paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea. This whole stretch is the Teacher telling you what is actually worth having, and it's not what shines. "A good name is better than fine perfume," he says (Ecclesiastes 7:1). Perfume fades by lunchtime, but a good name sticks around long after you walk out of the room.

So he points you toward the things that make you wise, even when they feel heavy. A house of mourning reminds the living that "death is the end of every man," and the living should take it to heart (Ecclesiastes 7:2). A wise man's rebuke stings, but it beats the song of fools (Ecclesiastes 7:5). Patience beats pride, and he says "anger settles in the lap of a fool" (Ecclesiastes 7:8, 9). I'm not saying never laugh, friend. I'm saying don't let the laughing be the only thing you do.

Then he sets the whole thing in God's hands. Wisdom is a shelter that "preserves the life of its owner" (Ecclesiastes 7:12), and God is the One who bends what you can't straighten (Ecclesiastes 7:13). So in the good day, be joyful. In the hard day, remember God made one along with the other, "so that a man cannot discover anything that will come after him" (Ecclesiastes 7:14). You don't have to see what's coming, baker. You just have to take wisdom with you into it.
